name: Identity politics
summary: Identity politics is political activity and theory founded in the shared experience of injustice of members of a social group, such as women, Black people, lesbians and gay men or Indigenous peoples. Its proponents start from analyses of group oppression and aim to reclaim or transform stigmatized identities and win self-determination, rather than organizing around a programme or party. The term was first used in the 1977 Combahee River Collective statement, which joined it to an analysis of interlocking racial, sexual, heterosexist and class oppression; it is rarely a full programme on economy or government.
scope: The strand the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines: politics of marginalized social groups rooted in shared experiences of injustice, with the Combahee River Collective statement as its germinal text and Crenshaw's intersectionality as its main elaboration. Answers rest on those texts and the entry's own account. It excludes the exclusionary nationalist and populist uses of the phrase that the entry mentions, the critics of identity politics, and the individual movements (feminism, Black nationalism, queer politics, Indigenous movements) that have their own entries.
